name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya
major_additions: present brick shikhara temple 5th-6th c. CE (Gupta); railings 1st c. BCE; restored 1880s
summary: Marking the spot of the Buddha's enlightenment, this is one of the earliest surviving all-brick temples in India and the prototype of the straight-edged pyramidal tower. Its 55 m shikhara, largely of the Gupta period over an Ashokan core, shows Indian temple-tower design at the very moment of its birth.

name: Barabar Caves (Lomas Rishi & Sudama)
dynasty: Maurya (Ashoka and grandson Dasharatha), for Ajivika ascetics
summary: India's oldest surviving rock-cut shrines, excavated under Emperor Ashoka with interiors polished to a mirror finish. The Lomas Rishi facade copies a wooden hut with a curved chaitya arch, the ancestor of a motif repeated on Indian temples for the next two thousand years.

name: Great Stupa, Sanchi
major_additions: enlarged with stone casing under Shungas 2nd c. BCE; four carved toranas 1st c. BCE (Satavahana)
summary: Commissioned by Ashoka, the Great Stupa is the best-preserved monument of India's earliest structural sacred architecture. Its hemispherical dome, railed processional path and four sculpted gateways established the vocabulary of the stupa across Asia.

name: Ajanta Caves
major_additions: second great phase of chaityas, viharas and murals c. 460-480 CE under Vakataka king Harishena
summary: Thirty caves cut into a horseshoe gorge trace Buddhist rock architecture from austere 2nd-century BCE prayer halls to the ornate pillared shrines of the 5th century CE. Their painted interiors are the finest surviving gallery of ancient Indian mural art.

name: Udayagiri & Khandagiri Caves
summary: Carved for Jain monks under King Kharavela, these twin hills hold India's earliest major Jain rock-cut complex, including the double-storeyed Rani Gumpha. Their sculpted friezes and the Hathigumpha inscription make them a cornerstone of early Kalinga art.

name: Karla Caves (Great Chaitya)
major_additions: Great Chaitya hall completed c. 120 CE
summary: The Great Chaitya at Karla is the largest and most perfectly finished early Buddhist prayer hall in India, its ribbed teak ceiling and colossal pillars faithfully translating timber construction into rock. It represents the climax of the Hinayana cave-temple tradition.

name: Temple 17, Sanchi
summary: This small flat-roofed sanctum with a four-pillared porch is textbook 'temple number one' — among the first free-standing stone temples ever built in India. Its plain cubical cella defines the germ from which all later Nagara and Dravida temples grew.

name: Udayagiri Caves (Vidisha)
summary: Dated by inscription to Chandragupta II's reign, these caves contain the celebrated colossal Varaha rescuing the earth goddess — the first great statement of Hindu imperial iconography in stone. They mark the moment Hindu worship acquired monumental architectural form.

name: Bhitargaon Brick Temple
summary: The oldest surviving terracotta-and-brick Hindu temple in India, Bhitargaon already carries a tall curved tower and true arches centuries before they became common. It is the crucial missing link between flat-roofed Gupta shrines and the soaring Nagara shikhara.

name: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
summary: This Vishnu temple is the first known panchayatana-plan temple and one of the earliest with a stone shikhara, its doorway and Anantashayana relief ranking among the masterpieces of Gupta sculpture. It shows the fully formed classical temple emerging around 500 CE.
sources: Vats, The Gupta Temple at Deogarh (ASI Memoir)

name: Durga Temple, Aihole
style: early Chalukya experimental (apsidal with Nagara tower)
summary: Aihole was the drawing board of Indian temple architecture, with over a hundred experimental shrines; its famous apsidal Durga Temple wraps a Buddhist chaitya plan in a Hindu colonnaded veranda. Here northern and southern temple ideas were tested side by side.
sources: UNESCO tentative list: Evolution of Temple Architecture, Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal

name: Elephanta Caves
dynasty: Kalachuri / Konkan Mauryas (attributed to Krishnaraja I)
summary: On an island in Mumbai harbour, the great cave of Shiva centres on the 6 m three-faced Sadashiva, one of the supreme achievements of Indian sculpture. Elephanta shows the Hindu cave temple at its most ambitious, a mandapa city carved from a single hill.

name: Badami Cave Temples
summary: Four caves above a red sandstone gorge — three Hindu and one Jain — carry a dated inscription of 578 CE, making them a fixed point in the chronology of Deccan art. Their Nataraja with eighteen arms is an icon of early Chalukya sculpture.

name: Ellora Caves (multi-faith complex)
major_additions: Buddhist caves c. 600-730; Hindu caves 6th-9th c.; Jain caves 9th-10th c.
summary: Thirty-four monasteries and temples cut over four centuries into a two-kilometre basalt scarp, Ellora is the encyclopaedia of Indian rock architecture and of religious coexistence. It records the handover from Buddhist cave halls to Hindu and Jain temple forms.

name: Pancha Rathas, Mahabalipuram
summary: Five free-standing temples each carved from a single boulder, the rathas are a sculptor's catalogue of South Indian roof forms — from thatched hut to multi-storeyed vimana. They are the experimental models from which the entire Dravida style was drawn.

name: Lakshana Devi Temple, Bharmour
summary: Founded by King Meruvarman around 700 CE, this cedar-wood shrine with its deeply carved doorway is among the oldest wooden temples surviving anywhere in the Himalaya. It preserves the timber tradition from which the hill-state pagoda temples later evolved.
sources: Hermann Goetz, Early Wooden Temples of Chamba

name: Kailasanathar Temple, Kanchipuram
summary: The first great structural stone temple of the Tamil country, wrapped in a wall of 58 miniature shrines and lion pilasters. Kailasanathar fixes the classic Dravida formula of vimana, mandapa and enclosing prakara that the Cholas would later monumentalise.

name: Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram
summary: Standing on the surf line of the Bay of Bengal, this twin-towered granite temple marks the Pallava leap from carving rock to building in dressed stone. Its slender tiered vimanas are the direct ancestors of every later South Indian temple tower.

name: Virupaksha Temple, Hampi
major_additions: nine-tier eastern gopuram, ranga-mandapa and courts added 1510 under Krishnadevaraya; continuously enlarged 14th-16th c.
summary: A small 7th-century Shiva shrine that grew into the ceremonial heart of the Vijayanagara empire, crowned by a 50 m gopuram. Uniquely at Hampi it has remained in unbroken worship, letting visitors experience a medieval imperial temple still alive with ritual.

name: Masrur Rock-cut Temples
summary: The only major monolithic rock-cut temple complex of the Himalaya, a cluster of Nagara shikharas hewn from a single sandstone ridge and mirrored in a sacred pool. Masrur shows the northern tower style translated, uniquely, into the carved-mountain idiom of Ellora.

name: Martand Sun Temple
style: Kashmiri (trefoil arches, peristyle court, pyramidal roofs)
summary: Lalitaditya's grand Sun temple, though now a ruin, defines the distinctive Kashmiri school — Gandharan-influenced fluted columns, trefoil doorways and an 84-column courtyard open to the Himalayan sky. It is the most ambitious classical monument of Kashmir.

name: Virupaksha Temple, Pattadakal
style: Dravida (Chalukya; site pairs Nagara and Dravida temples)
dynasty: Chalukya (Queen Lokamahadevi, wife of Vikramaditya II)
summary: Built by a queen to celebrate victory over the Pallavas, this is the largest of Pattadakal's ten temples, where northern and southern styles stand deliberately side by side. The site is the graduation hall of Chalukya architecture and the model for Ellora's Kailasa.

name: Osian Temples (Sachiya Mata & Harihara group)
major_additions: Sachiya Mata temple rebuilt 12th c.; Jain Mahavira temple enlarged 10th-11th c.
summary: This desert oasis preserves the earliest group of Hindu and Jain temples in Rajasthan, their balconied walls and ornate toranas defining the Pratihara school. Osian is where the ornament-rich western Indian idiom that later flowered at Khajuraho and Dilwara began.
sources: Dhaky, Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture

name: Kailasa Temple (Cave 16), Ellora
summary: The largest monolithic structure on earth: a complete two-storey Dravida temple, courtyard, gateway and life-size elephants released from the hillside by removing some 200,000 tonnes of rock, top downward. It is the audacious climax of India's rock-cut tradition.

name: Vettuvan Koil, Kalugumalai
summary: Called 'heaven of the sculptors', this unfinished Pandya monolith was carved from the top down, leaving its exquisitely finished vimana crown rising from raw rock. It uniquely freezes the construction process, revealing exactly how monolithic temples were made.

name: Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangam
major_additions: expanded by Chola, Pandya, Hoysala, Vijayanagara and Nayaka rulers; 72 m Rajagopuram completed 1987
dynasty: Chola and successive South Indian dynasties
protection: active temple trust (TN HR&CE); UNESCO Asia-Pacific conservation award
summary: The largest functioning temple complex in India, a 63-hectare temple-town of seven concentric walled enclosures that swallowed the city around it. Srirangam demonstrates the final evolutionary stage of the Dravida temple: from single shrine to sacred urbanism.

name: Lakshmana Temple, Khajuraho
summary: Consecrated c. 954, this is the earliest fully developed Khajuraho temple, its high platform, clustered shikhara and sculpture-saturated walls announcing the mature central Indian Nagara style. Its friezes preview the sensuous exuberance the site is famous for.

name: Mukteshwar Temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Nicknamed the 'gem of Odishan architecture', this compact 10th-century shrine introduces the sculpted stone torana archway and the fully articulated Kalinga deul-jagamohana pair. It is the stylistic bridge between early Bhubaneswar shrines and the giant Lingaraj.

name: Gommateshwara (Bahubali), Shravanabelagola
major_additions: Mahamastakabhisheka anointing held every 12 years since 981; surrounding bastis 10th-17th c.
style: monolithic colossus with Jain basti complex
summary: The 17.4 m Bahubali, carved from a single granite outcrop atop Vindhyagiri hill in 981, is one of the largest free-standing monolithic statues in the world. With its hilltop bastis it embodies the Jain contribution of colossal open-air sacred sculpture.

name: Lingaraj Temple, Bhubaneswar
major_additions: nata-mandira and bhoga-mandapa added 12th c. under Eastern Gangas
summary: Its 55 m curvilinear tower dominating Bhubaneswar's skyline, Lingaraj is the grandest living monument of the Kalinga school, with the full four-hall axial sequence later repeated at Puri and Konark. Worship has continued here without interruption for a millennium.
sources: K.C. Panigrahi, Archaeological Remains at Bhubaneswar

name: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur
major_additions: Subrahmanya shrine 17th c. (Nayaka); Amman shrine 13th c. (Pandya)
summary: Completed in 1010, Rajaraja's 'Great Temple' raised a 66 m all-granite vimana capped by an 80-tonne crowning stone — the tallest structure of its age in India. It is the supreme statement of imperial Dravida architecture and Chola engineering.

name: Sun Temple, Modhera
summary: Aligned so the equinox sun strikes its sanctum, Modhera pairs a lace-carved temple and dance hall with a spectacular stepped tank of 108 miniature shrines. It is the Solanki dynasty's finest showcase of the ornate Maru-Gurjara style.

name: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple, Khajuraho
summary: The climax of the Nagara style: 84 subsidiary turrets cascade up its 31 m shikhara like a rising mountain range, over walls carrying nearly 900 sculptures. Kandariya Mahadeva is the most perfectly composed temple of medieval north India.

name: Dilwara Temples (Vimal Vasahi & Luna Vasahi), Mount Abu
major_additions: Luna Vasahi added 1230 by ministers Vastupala and Tejapala
summary: Behind plain exteriors lie the most virtuosic marble interiors ever carved in India — pendant lotus ceilings so thin they are translucent. Dilwara represents the Maru-Gurjara style, and Jain patronage, at their absolute technical peak.
sources: Dhaky, Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture

name: Gangaikonda Cholapuram (Brihadisvara Temple)
summary: Built by Rajendra I to crown his new capital after his Ganges expedition, its 55 m vimana answers Thanjavur's with a softer, concave curve and some of the finest Chola sculpture, including the famed Chandesha-anugraha panel. It shows the imperial style refined rather than merely repeated.

name: Rani ki Vav, Patan
summary: A queen's memorial stepwell descending seven storeys, lined with over 500 large sculptures of Vishnu's avatars — effectively a temple built upside-down into the earth. It shows Solanki temple art applied to India's unique water architecture.

name: Palitana Temples, Shatrunjaya Hill
major_additions: most of the 800+ shrines rebuilt 16th c. onward after earlier destructions
dynasty: Jain merchant patrons over nine centuries
summary: Over 800 marble temples climb Shatrunjaya hill in fortified clusters, built and rebuilt by Jain merchants for nine hundred years. Palitana is the world's largest temple-city and the ultimate expression of collective, trans-generational temple building.

name: Vadakkunnathan Temple, Thrissur
major_additions: shrines, koothambalam and murals renewed 15th-17th c.; conservation awarded UNESCO prize 2015
style: Kerala (multi-shrine walled kshetra, sloping copper roofs)
summary: Set in a nine-acre walled green at the heart of Thrissur, this Shiva temple is the archetype of the Kerala style — circular and square shrines under tiered timber-and-copper roofs, with a magnificent koothambalam theatre hall. It shows how the monsoon coast evolved its own gabled temple idiom.

name: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
major_additions: gopuram rebuilt 14th c. (Vijayanagara)
summary: Begun in 1117 to mark Vishnuvardhana's victories, Belur's star-planned soapstone temple carries the celebrated madanika bracket figures, carved with jeweller's precision. It opens the Hoysala chapter, where sculpture and architecture fuse completely.
sources: UNESCO WHC (whc.unesco.org/en/list/1670 - Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas)

name: Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu
summary: The largest Hoysala temple, its twin shrines wrapped in an unbroken 200 m band of friezes — elephants, epics and deities in thousands — often called the most richly sculpted exterior in India. Halebidu is Hoysala art at maximum density.
sources: UNESCO WHC (Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, 2023)

name: Jagannath Temple, Puri
major_additions: nata-mandira and bhoga-mandapa added later 12th-13th c.; kitchen complex among world's largest
protection: active temple trust (Shri Jagannath Temple Administration); state protected
summary: One of Hinduism's four dhams, its 65 m tower presides over the Rath Yatra, the world's most famous chariot festival. Puri shows the Kalinga temple as a living civic institution, feeding tens of thousands daily from its vast kitchens.

name: Airavatesvara Temple, Darasuram
summary: Conceived as 'perpetual entertainment', this compact late-Chola temple features a mandapa shaped as a stone chariot with wheels and singing steps that ring musically. It shows the imperial style turning from colossal scale to exquisite refinement.

name: Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple, Palampet
summary: Named after its sculptor Ramappa, this temple pairs mirror-polished basalt bracket figures with a vimana of porous 'floating' bricks light enough to float on water, over earthquake-resistant sandbox foundations. It is the engineering masterpiece of the Kakatiyas, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

name: Meenakshi Amman Temple, Madurai
major_additions: most gopurams, thousand-pillar hall and tank 16th-17th c. under Nayakas (Tirumala Nayaka)
summary: A 14-towered temple-city dedicated jointly to goddess Meenakshi and Shiva, its gateway gopurams teeming with thousands of painted stucco figures. Madurai represents the final Dravida phase, when soaring gateways and vast pillared halls eclipsed the central shrine.

name: Konark Sun Temple
major_additions: main deul collapsed by 19th c.; jagamohana sealed and conserved 1903
summary: The entire temple is conceived as the Sun god's chariot, riding on twelve pairs of exquisitely carved stone wheels drawn by seven horses — the wheels doubling as working sundials. Konark is the audacious grand finale of the Kalinga school.

name: Keshava Temple, Somanathapura
dynasty: Hoysala (commander Somanatha Dandanayaka under Narasimha III)
summary: The last and most perfectly finished great Hoysala temple: three star-shaped shrines on a single platform, every surface carved in disciplined horizontal bands. Somanathapura closes the Hoysala story as its most complete surviving statement.
sources: UNESCO WHC (Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, 2023)

name: Vittala Temple, Hampi
major_additions: greatly enlarged 1513-1565 under Krishnadevaraya; stone chariot and musical-pillar mandapas 16th c.
summary: The showpiece of Vijayanagara architecture, famous for its granite stone chariot and halls of slender 'musical' pillars that resonate when struck. Vittala displays the empire's signature open composite mandapas at their most theatrical.

name: Ranakpur Adinatha Temple
dynasty: Jain merchant Dharna Shah under Rana Kumbha of Mewar
summary: A four-faced marble temple whose forest of 1,444 pillars — no two alike — fills 29 halls under 80 domes with shifting light. Ranakpur proves the Maru-Gurjara tradition still ascendant in the 15th century, at architectural full complexity.

name: Hidimba Devi Temple, Manali
summary: Rising in four timber tiers from a deodar forest, this 1553 shrine encloses a natural rock worshipped as the goddess Hidimba. It is the best-known example of the Himalayan pagoda style, where cedar wood and sloping roofs answer snow instead of sun.

name: Kamakhya Temple, Guwahati
major_additions: rebuilt 1565 on 8th-10th c. remains; shrines added by Ahom kings 17th-18th c.
style: Nilachal (hybrid: hemispherical dome on cruciform base)
summary: The greatest of the Shakti pithas, rebuilt in 1565 in the 'Nilachal' style invented here — a beehive dome over a cruciform plan that became the template for temples across Assam. It anchors the distinctive northeastern chapter of Indian temple building.

name: Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
major_additions: rebuilt and expanded 1731-1750s under Marthanda Varma; 30 m seven-tier gopuram completed 18th c.
summary: Home of the reclining Padmanabha and famed for its treasure vaults, this temple uniquely fuses a Tamil-style gopuram with Kerala's sloping roofs and colonnades. It records the meeting of the two great southern building traditions on the Malabar coast.

name: Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), Amritsar
major_additions: rebuilt 1764 after destruction; marble cladding and gold gilding 1802-1830 under Maharaja Ranjit Singh
style: Sikh (fusion of Indo-Islamic and Rajput idioms)
dynasty: Sikh Gurus (Guru Arjan Dev); Sikh Empire (Ranjit Singh)
summary: Set at the centre of a sacred pool and entered by descending steps, with four doors open to all, the Golden Temple gave Sikhism its own architectural language of domes, chhatris and gilded surfaces. Its layout deliberately inverts the exclusivity of the hilltop shrine.

name: Terracotta Temples of Bishnupur (Shyam Rai & Jor Bangla)
style: Bengal chala-ratna (curved thatch-form roofs, terracotta panels)
summary: In brick-rich, stone-poor Bengal, the Mallas translated the village thatched hut into temple form, curving their cornices and sheathing walls in narrative terracotta plaques of the Krishna legend. Bishnupur is the definitive gallery of this regional style.
sources: UNESCO tentative list: Temples at Bishnupur

name: Sivadol, Sivasagar
style: Ahom (tall shikhara on Nilachal lines, golden kalasha)
dynasty: Ahom (Queen Ambika for King Siva Singha)
summary: Rising 32 m beside the great Borpukhuri tank, Sivadol is claimed as the tallest Shiva temple of its kind in India and the finest monument of the Ahom dynasty. It shows the Assamese dol style at full maturity on the eve of the colonial era.

name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple, Varanasi
major_additions: domes gilded 1839 with gold from Ranjit Singh; Vishwanath Corridor to the Ganga completed 2021
dynasty: Rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore (Maratha)
summary: The present temple of Shiva as Lord of Kashi was rebuilt in 1780 by queen Ahilyabai Holkar, emblematic of the great Maratha-era wave of temple restoration across north India. Its gilded spires and new river corridor link medieval piety to 21st-century urban design.

name: Dakshineswar Kali Temple, Kolkata
summary: Built by the philanthropist Rani Rashmoni and sanctified by Ramakrishna's ministry, this riverside Kali temple crowns the Bengali navaratna style with nine spires over a colonnaded courtyard of twelve Shiva shrines. It shows temple architecture entering the modern era under new, non-royal patrons.

name: Laxminarayan (Birla) Mandir, Delhi
dynasty: Birla industrialist family (arch. Sris Chandra Chatterjee)
summary: The first of the famous Birla Mandirs, completed in 1939 and opened by Mahatma Gandhi on condition it admit all castes. Its concrete-and-marble revivalist towers announced industrial patronage and social reform as the new forces in Indian temple building.

name: Somnath Temple, Prabhas Patan
major_additions: current temple consecrated 1951 on site of shrines destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly since at least the 10th c.
dynasty: Somnath Trust (initiative of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel; arch. Prabhashankar Sompura)
summary: Rebuilt after Independence in the Chaulukya style by the hereditary Sompura temple architects, Somnath resurrects a shrine razed many times over a millennium. It stands for the 20th-century revival of classical temple craft as an act of national renewal.

name: Swaminarayan Akshardham, Delhi
style: modern traditional (pink sandstone and marble, shastra-based, no structural steel)
summary: Opened in 2005 after 11,000 artisans revived shastra-prescribed techniques — carving 234 pillars and nine domes without structural steel. Akshardham demonstrates that the full medieval craft tradition can still be mobilised at monumental scale today.

name: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Mandir, Ayodhya
major_additions: consecrated 22 January 2024; upper floors and 732 m parikrama wall completing through 2026
style: Nagara (Gurjara-Chalukya mode, pink Bansi Paharpur sandstone)
dynasty: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust (arch. Chandrakant Sompura)
summary: Consecrated in 2024, this three-storey, 161-foot Nagara temple was designed by the Sompura family in the Gurjara-Chalukya idiom, built without steel and engineered for a thousand-year life. It is the newest landmark in the unbroken 2,000-year evolution of the Indian temple.
